senses.gloss:
caraṇavyūha
(‘formation or arrangement of caraṇas’)
------------------------------------------
Vedic seers have accepted the princi-ple that revelation is a continuing process. Hence the volume of revealed mantras that constitute the वेदस् went on growing, gradually reaching such levels that were beyond the normal ranges of human memory. It thus became necessary to compile index-works and appendices that would help the memorization process or locate the needed information. Anukrama-ṇikās and pariśiṣṭas are such works. The caraṇavyūhas belong to the latter group.
Among the two caraṇavyūhas extant, the first belongs to शुक्ल यजुर्वेद and is said to be the work of कात्यायन. This lists the various शाखास् or branches of that Veda. The work as it obtains today seems to be of later origin and its list is incomplete.
The second one is the 49th परिशिष्ट of the अथर्ववेद. It mentions the chief characteristics of the अथर्ववेद and gives the number of the mantras as 12,380 included in 2000 sūktas. The ṛṣis (sages) and देवतास् (deities) of the mantras are also mentioned.
For each śākhā of the वेदस्, the caraṇavyūhas mention the names of the related ब्राह्मणस्, आरण्यकस्, Sūtras, उपवेद etc.
There is a work called चरणव्यूह-sūtra attributed to शौनक giving the details of the four वेदस्, their śākhas and allied literature in five chapters.
See also ANUKRAMAṆĪ and PARIŚIṢṬA.

Carmaṇvatī
(‘with hides’)
------------------------------------------
Rantideva, an ancient king, performed several sacrifices in which many animals had been immolated. The hides of these had been heaped in one place. A river is said to have started flowing from there and it was christened ‘Carmaṇvatī’. Drupada’s (father of द्रौपदी and king of Pāñcāla) kingdom extended up to this river.
It is generally identified with the modern Chambal river that rises about 14 kms. (9 miles) south-west of Mhow (in Madhya Pradesh) and joins the river यमुना 40 kms. (25 miles) south of Etawah town in Uttar Pradesh.

caraliṅga
(‘the moving symbol [of God’)
------------------------------------------
The cult of वीरशैविस्म्, with its philosophy of शक्ति-viśiṣṭādvaita, took a definite shape during the middle ages in the province of Karnataka. But it is rooted in the ancient schools of शैविस्म्.
According to it, ‘Sthala’ or the Absolute (equivalent of ब्रह्मन्) with its ‘Śakti’ or inherent power divides itself into ‘aṅga’ (the जीव) and ‘liṅga’ (Para or परमात्मन्). ‘Caraliṅga’, also called ‘jaṅgamaliṅga’, is one of the aspects of this लिङ्ग. Since the human body is animated by परमात्मन् and is capable of movement (cara or जङ्गम = that which moves), it is called ‘caraliṅga’ or ‘jaṅgamaliṅga’.
For details see ŚAKTIVIŚIṢṬĀDVAITA and VĪRAŚAIVISM.

Cārvāka-darśana
(‘philosophy of those who speak sweetly’)
------------------------------------------
Schools of Indian मतेरिअलिस्म्, of various hues and shades, are generally called Cārvākadarśana or Lokāyatamata. Whether there was a real founder of this school by name Cārvāka is difficult to prove; probably not. The name of बृहस्पति, son of लोक, is sometimes mentioned as the founder of this system.
The word ‘Cārvāka’ itself has been interpreted as ‘one who speaks sweetly’ (from cāru = sweet, vāk = speech) or as one who lives ‘to eat’ (from carv = to eat or enjoy). The term ‘Lokāyata’ means ‘restricted to the world of common experience’. Both these names refer to the nature of this system.
There are no extant basic texts of this school. Information has to be gleaned from various other works which state these views sometimes even quoting from their works, with the sole purpose of contradicting and criticizing them.
The Cārvāka system accepts प्रत्यक्ष or direct perception as the only pramāṇa or valid source of knowledge, rejecting even अनुमान or inference. Consequently it admits of only four elements—pṛthvī (earth), ap (water), तेजस् (fire) and वायु (air)—as the fundamental substances constituting the world. It denies the existence of God and सोउल्. चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्, according to it, is a chemical product of the combination of the elements that make up the body. काम or pleasure here and now, is the only goal of life. अर्थ or wealth is a means to it. One is advised to get the maximum pleasure out of life, before it is too late. In this process no attention need be paid to धर्म, any moral or ethical scruples. मोक्ष or emancipation is a myth. Since death is the end of life and there is no rebirth, life need not be ‘all labour’ except for what is necessary to get pleasure.
The Cārvākas are sometimes classified into two groups: dhūrtas or the crass ones and suśikṣitas or the cultured ones. The former are base materialists interested only in the crude satisfaction of beastly instincts. The latter as represented by वात्स्यायन and others, accept धर्म or righteousness also along with अर्थ and काम, and stress the need for self-control and discipline in life.
Whatever be their defect, the Cārvākas have certainly forced the later philosophers to give up dogmatism and spurred their free thinking.

caramaśloka
(‘the final or concluding verse’)
------------------------------------------
Rāmānuja’s (A. D. 1017-1137) teachings are twofold. The philosophical aspect is known as Viśiṣṭādvaita Vedānta. The practical, religious, aspect is called श्रीवैष्णविस्म्.
Śrīvaiṣṇavism lays great emphasis on भक्ति (devotion to God) and प्रपत्ति (self-surrender) as the two parallel means of attaining मोक्ष or लिबेरतिओन्.
Prapatti depends upon receiving the रहस्यत्रय (‘the three secrets’) from a qualified preceptor and practising the same.
They are: aṣṭākṣarīmantra, dvaya-मन्त्र and चरमश्लोक. (See AṢṬĀKṢARĪ and DVAYAMANTRA for details.)
The चरमश्लोक is the 66th verse in the last chapter of the भगवद्गीता (18.66). Though it is not the last in the section, since it contains the ultimate or final (= carama) message of श्रीकृष्ण, it has been designated as such.
The verse is:
sarvadharmān parityajya
māmekaṁ śaraṇam vraja ।
ahaṁ tvā sarvapāpebhyo
mokṣayiṣyāmi mā śucaḥ ॥
(‘Abandoning all dharmas [human efforts at moral and spiritual upliftment] come to Me as the only Refuge. Grieve not; I will deliver you from all sins’)
See also RAHASYATRAYASĀRA.

caraka
(‘one who moves’)
------------------------------------------
The word is used to indicate a spy as well as the saṁnyāsin both of whom are given to much movement.
As regards चरक, the great teacher of आयुर्वेद, see CARAKASAṀHITĀ.

caraṇa
(‘that by which one moves’)
------------------------------------------
The word ‘caraṇa’ has been used in several senses like: foot, a quarter of verse, pillar of a temple and part of a musical composition (in Carnatic मुसिच्).
In the Vedic terminology, it refers to a branch of the Veda (in a much larger sense) and the group of people who study it. It includes not only the particular śākhā (the branch or recension of Veda traditionally allotted to them for specialization) but also its allied literature like the law-books.
In बुद्धिस्म् it refers to the eight aspects of character like fearlessness and self-control, fit to be cultivated.

Caraka-saṁhitā
(‘compilation of चरक’)
------------------------------------------
Caraka and सुश्रुत are the two brightest स्तर्स् in the firmament of आयुर्वेद or the Science of Life. Due to several reasons including the destruction or plundering of valuable manuscripts by the various hordes, invading this country, it is very difficult to know about their period or original works.
The Hindu traditions which ascribe the origin of आयुर्वेद to the creator ब्रह्मा himself mention about the sage आत्रेय पुनर्वसु and his brilliant disciple अग्निवेश. चरक is said to be the disciple of अग्निवेश. Since his name has been mentioned in the epic महाभारत, some scholars assign him to the period 1400 B.C. Others however opine that चरक was the court physician of Kāniṣka (3rd cent. A.D.), the Kuśāna king.
His work Carakasaṁhitā, as it has come down to us today, is undoubtedly a much revised edition. Dṛḍhabala, a prominent writer (of आयुर्वेद), is said to have edited the earlier work and added several sections since the original was incomplete. It consists of eight prakaraṇas or sections divided into thirty chapters. It is exclusively a book of medicine and not of surgery.
The contents of the eight prakaraṇas, very briefly, are as follows:
Sūtrasthāna: origin of medicines; duties of the physician; use of medicines; cure of diseases; materia medica; diet.
Nidānasthāna: curing of diseases like fever, tumours, diabetes, leprosy, tuberculosis, manias and epilepsy.
Vimānasthāna: epidemics; nature of ड़ोओद्; symptoms and diagnosis of diseases; use of medicines; peculiarities of the fluids of the body.
Śarīrasthāna: nature of the सोउल्; conception; varieties of species; qualities of elements; description of the body; connection of body and the सोउल्.
Indriyasthāna: organs of senses and their diseases; loss of strength and death.
Cikitsāsthāna: diseases like dropsy, swelling, piles, jaundice, asthma, dysentery and effects of poisons; means of improving health and enjoying long life.
Kalpasthāna: emetics, purgatives, antidotes and medical charms.
Siddhisthāna: evacuating medi-cines, injections, abscesses and other topics.
It is a remarkable work written in the campū (mixture of prose and poetry) style. Even mental illnesses and epidemic diseases have been dealt with in detail. It has been translated into Persian and Arabic languages in the 8th cent. A. D. There are 17 commentaries on it in Sanskrit.
See also ĀYURVEDA and SUŚRUTA-SAṀHITĀ.

Caraṇadāsa
(‘the servant of [God’s] feet’)
------------------------------------------
He is the founder of the Caraṇadāsī sect that goes in his name. He lived in the 18th century. He was born at Dehara near Delhi. His गुरु was Sukhadevadāsa. He founded his sect when he was about 35 years of age and lived for about 78 years. The followers of this sect are generally found in Delhi, Haryana, western Uttar Pradesh and northern Rajasthan.
He lived mostly in Alwar and taught devotion to कृष्ण. The eleventh book of the भागवत was the basic text for his teachings. He wrote several works on योग and भक्ति. Two of his distinguished disciples were women: Sahajobāī and Dayābāī.
His followers sing bhajans in honour of कृष्ण.

caru
(‘that which is eaten [by the gods]’)
------------------------------------------
Caru is one of the several materials normally used in वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस् for oblation. It is a kind of porridge prepared from unpounded rice or barley grains by cooking it in water and mixing it with butter or milk. It is used for oblation and also consumed by four of the priests specified in the sacrificial works. It is sometimes substituted for पुरोडाश (a kind of rice-cake used for offering) in the subsidiary or modified rites called ‘vikṛtis’. The vessel used for keeping or serving it is also called चरु and sometimes as carusthālī.
See also PUROḌĀŚA.
